content.p: On the damp, foggy morning of 11 November 1778, a column of Seneca and other Iroquois warriors, Loyalist rangers and a few British regulars came out of the mist above Cherry Valley, a farming settlement in the New York backcountry. Its Continental garrison, commanded by Colonel Ichabod Alden, had been warned for days that an attack was coming. Alden dismissed the warnings. Within hours he was dead, the settlement's houses were burning, and men, women and children were being killed or marched off as captives.

The palisaded fort at the centre of the village, Fort Alden, was never taken. The killing happened in the houses around it, while the soldiers inside watched. The American Battlefield Trust counts it among the harshest atrocities of the whole war. The raid's overall commander, Captain Walter Butler, was a young Loyalist officer whom some sources describe as driven by revenge, and the sources still disagree over how much of the blame belongs to him, to his Seneca allies and to the Mohawk war leader Joseph Brant. The raid was followed, the next year, by the Sullivan Expedition against the Iroquois.
content.h2: A settlement in the line of fire
content.p: Cherry Valley lay about sixty miles west of Albany. Revolutionary War Journal says four families first settled it in 1738; the Encyclopedia of the American Revolution dates the first farm to the summer of 1740, when John Lindsay arrived from New York City. Either way it was small and isolated, and it had lived on good terms with its Mohawk neighbours. Its people sided with the Patriot cause in the early months of the revolution, and by 1776 they were petitioning for soldiers. A fortified house belonging to Colonel Samuel Campbell served as a refuge for the inhabitants.

By 1778 the war in the north had turned into a frontier war. After the British defeat at Saratoga the year before, the offensive work in upstate New York was left largely to Loyalist and Native American raiders, who struck at the Mohawk Valley settlements that kept feeding the American army. Cherry Valley sat on the edge of that country. In the months before the attack, Revolutionary War Journal records a run of raids: Wyoming in Pennsylvania in early July, German Flatts on the Mohawk in September, and an American counter-raid by Colonel Thomas Hartley up the Susquehanna. The encyclopedia entry adds that Patriots destroyed Unadilla, Brant's base, on 8 October. The sources name revenge for these blows to Iroquois villages as one motive for striking Cherry Valley.

Alden's 7th Massachusetts Regiment reached the valley in 1778, in July by the encyclopedia's account and on 6 June by Revolutionary War Journal's. The encyclopedia gives his strength as about 250 men and Revolutionary War Journal as about 300. The soldiers built a stockade with cannon, which was named Fort Alden in mid-August. Several of the sources are harsh about the colonel. The encyclopedia says he "has been much criticized as a poor officer" and that his men had no experience of frontier warfare; History.com says he was strategically out of his depth.
content.h2: The man who led the raid
content.p: Walter Butler, the captain in command, was the son of John Butler, who directed Loyalist operations from Fort Niagara and whose regiment was popularly called Butler's Rangers. According to the American Battlefield Trust, Walter had studied law in Albany and was arrested in August 1777 while secretly recruiting for the Loyalist cause near German Flatts. Benedict Arnold had him convicted of espionage and sentenced to death, and old classmates won him a stay of execution and the time to escape. The Trust says Butler apparently disliked Brant, with whom he had to work.

The My Revolutionary War site tells the story more vividly: Butler, it says, spent months in a miserable Albany jail, escaped to Niagara with the help of family and sympathisers, and swore to take revenge. That is the site's account of his motive, not a fact established by a court or by Butler's own words. The same page says Brant was angry at being placed under Butler's command and had lost his own base at Oquaga to American raiders. The two men and their followers met near Tioga and picked Cherry Valley as the target.
content.h2: The warning that Alden waved away
content.p: Patriot intelligence was accurate. The encyclopedia entry says that on 6 November a message came from Fort Stanwix, passing on word from friendly Indians of a large gathering of Indians and Loyalists at Tioga, where Walter Butler was present, and where the decision to attack Cherry Valley had been taken. My Revolutionary War dates the message 8 November and quotes it: an Oneida had reported that "young Butler was to head the Tories."

The settlers, hearing of it, asked to move their belongings into the new fort. Alden refused. According to the encyclopedia, he said the intelligence was probably wrong and that valuables inside Fort Alden would tempt his soldiers to steal. My Revolutionary War has him calling the report an "idle Indian rumor". Revolutionary War Journal says General Edward Hand, then commanding the Army of the North at Albany, also visited and urged precautions, and that Alden ignored him too. Alden and his officers, the same account says, were living in private houses outside the fort.

He did send out scouts. A ten-man party that went down the Susquehanna was captured on the morning of 10 November, the encyclopedia says, after its members slept around a fire. The same entry says the prisoners told Butler and Brant that the rebel officers were quartered outside the fort, and that this shaped the plan. Revolutionary War Journal adds that one of the scouts, Robert Bray, was killed, and that it is believed a captive talked.

Several inches of snow fell on the night of 10 and 11 November, and by morning rain and a thick haze hid the approaching force. The plan, in the encyclopedia's account, was to hit the officers' billets first and then the fort. Around eleven, though some accounts say as early as ten, the Indians fired on a farmer riding toward the fort. He was wounded but reached the village and raised the alarm.

What happened next is told differently by different sources. In the encyclopedia's version, the Rangers halted to check their weapons while a Seneca advance party raced ahead to the Wells house, about 400 yards from the fort, where Alden was lodged with his second in command, Lieutenant Colonel William Stacy, and a headquarters company. My Revolutionary War says the Rangers' powder was wet, and adds that some reports claim the pause was deliberate, to let the Senecas lead. It also says Butler stopped the Rangers on purpose and made no effort to restrain the Senecas, an interpretation the page itself offers rather than a proven fact. According to Revolutionary War Journal, the Seneca chief Little Beard led the warriors who surrounded the Wells house.

Alden ran for the fort and did not make it. How he died is told in several ways. Nelson Greene's history of the Mohawk Valley, quoting an earlier local historian, says an Indian pursued him, threw a tomahawk that struck his head, and killed and scalped him. My Revolutionary War names Brant as the man who threw the tomahawk, after Alden had turned and tried to fire a pistol that misfired. Revolutionary War Journal says most accounts have him almost at the fort gates and that reports differ over whether he tried to shoot. Stacy was captured. Accounts of his capture say Brant stepped in as he was about to be killed; Revolutionary War Journal adds the story that Stacy, a Freemason, appealed to Brant as a fellow Mason.

The fort's gates closed. The raiders had no cannon to break the palisade, and grapeshot from the fort's guns discouraged any rush. A garrison journal quoted by Revolutionary War Journal says the enemy "after three hours retreated without success of taking the fort"; the encyclopedia gives the withdrawal time as 3:30 p.m. Revolutionary War Journal describes the Loyalists keeping the fort under watch while the Iroquois spread through the village, and says the garrison could do no more than watch and listen from the ramparts.

Of the roughly forty homes in the settlement, the encyclopedia says, only six were occupied when the raiders turned on them. The most-told episode is the destruction of the household at the Wells house. The sources do not agree on who died there. Revolutionary War Journal counts twelve dead, among them Wells, his wife, her mother, four children, Wells's brother John and sister Jane, and three servants. Greene's history, in the extract on the library page, says the entire household was killed: the couple, a brother and a sister, three children and three servants. My Revolutionary War names three sons and a daughter. Greene and My Revolutionary War agree that one son, away at school in Schenectady, survived.

Two accounts tell of a young woman who fled the house and was struck down even though a Loyalist who had once served the family stepped in front of her and claimed she was his sister. Greene calls her a daughter of Wells; My Revolutionary War calls her Eleanor, Wells's sister, and names Little Beard as her killer.

Elsewhere in the valley, the Reverend Samuel Dunlop was spared by the Seneca chief Little Aaron, who had once heard him preach, but his wife was killed. Hugh Mitchell hid in the woods and returned to find his wife and three of his children dead; a fourth child, a girl, was still alive. According to My Revolutionary War, a Loyalist sergeant named Newberry then killed her. Revolutionary War Journal gives the same name, adds that a fellow Ranger, Rolf Hare, was with him, and says both men were hanged the next year at Canajoharie for their part in the attack. Colonel Campbell was away from home; his wife and children were taken prisoner. The encyclopedia credits a sortie from the fort, led by Captain John McDonnell, with saving many settlers who were sheltering in the woods.

The prisoners were marched out of the valley in a cold November storm. They camped about two miles away, according to Greene's history, and on the way came the announcement that the women and children would be sent back. In the encyclopedia's count the raiders departed with seventy-one captives, and most were let go the following day. Mrs. Cannon, Mrs. Campbell's elderly mother, could not keep up and was killed by the roadside, according to Greene and to My Revolutionary War, which says an Indian tomahawked her.

Butler kept two women and their children: Mrs. Campbell with her four children, and Mrs. James Moore with three daughters, the encyclopedia says. Its explanation is that his mother and wife, with the wives of other Loyalist officers, were held by Patriots in Albany, and he wanted hostages. My Revolutionary War says it was his mother and younger children who had been left behind, and that he held the women to punish their husbands. Butler also wrote to General Philip Schuyler on 12 November. In the letter, quoted by My Revolutionary War, he said he had "done everything in my power to restrain the fury of the Indians from hurting women and children", that his Indians were incensed at the destruction of their village at Unadilla, and that if his family stayed in custody he and his father would no longer take such pains.

The women and children held in Iroquois hands were taken west. Revolutionary War Journal says Mrs. Campbell spent about a year at the Seneca village of Kanedaseago before being moved to Niagara, where she waited nearly to the end of the war for an exchange. Her seven-year-old son, separated from her, was found at Montreal. By then he had forgotten English and spoke an Iroquois language, most likely Seneca. The captured soldiers were taken to Niagara, and Stacy was exchanged in time to join the Sullivan Expedition.

No source offers a single tidy figure. The garrison's quartermaster, Lieutenant William McKendry, identified Alden and thirteen privates among the soldiers killed, Revolutionary War Journal reports, and other reports give sixteen. The same page puts the civilian dead at thirty-two found bodies, with some accounts saying forty. The American Battlefield Trust gives thirteen to sixteen soldiers and thirty civilians, with seventy more taken captive. History.com says the attackers killed more than forty Patriots and took at least seventy prisoners. Greene's history of the Mohawk Valley gives forty-eight killed and forty made prisoners in its chapter summary, though a note on the library's web page warns that later research has superseded some of the book's information.

Help arrived late. Revolutionary War Journal, citing Greene, says Continental troops under Colonel James Gordon and Mohawk Valley militia under Colonel Klock reached the fort about two hours after the raiders had gone. They helped gather the survivors who had hidden in the woods and buried the dead in a common grave in the village cemetery. The settlement was abandoned: little was left but the fort, the church and a few houses, and the survivors mostly went to the Mohawk Valley. The fort was occupied until the following summer.

The question of responsibility was disputed within weeks and has not been closed. In the encyclopedia's account, the Patriot prisoners blamed Butler for the murder of about twenty-four civilians and credited Brant with stopping the killing of women and children. The American Battlefield Trust says Butler later blamed Brant for ordering the attack, but that some contemporary witnesses say Brant tried to stop the violence or was not present at all. Revolutionary War Journal says it was later learned that Brant and Butler tried and failed to restrain the Senecas, and quotes the historian Barbara Graymont, who judged Butler's failure, as the expedition's overall commander, to look to civilian safety "criminally incompetent". Butler himself wrote that he could not prevent some women and children falling victim to the Indians, and added that he had spent most of his time guarding the fort.

My Revolutionary War argues the opposite view of Brant, saying early documents show he was not in command and did his best to save inhabitants, and that Walter Butler was in command. It also reports that Butler's father, on hearing of the Wells killings, said he would have gone miles on his hands and knees to save that family, and accused Brant of secretly ordering the massacre to shame his son. That accusation is the elder Butler's, as the page reports it. The Encyclopedia of the American Revolution takes a military view: it calls the raid a brilliant coup carried out in the face of great difficulties, and says American accounts dwell on its horrors largely because of the incompetence of the American leadership.

Cherry Valley, with Wyoming and German Flatts, became one of the three attacks of 1778 that Revolutionary War Journal says were each called a massacre. The page says news of Cherry Valley appeared in the Boston Gazette on 7 December 1778, naming only the officers killed or missing. The Continental Congress, the American Battlefield Trust says, ordered Washington to launch a retaliatory campaign. The Trust says the 1779 Sullivan Expedition destroyed more than 40 Iroquois villages, but that violence on the frontier continued until the end of the war. Revolutionary War Journal describes the campaign as amounting to genocide and says half of the Iroquois driven west would die of starvation and cold.

Walter Butler did not survive the war. The American Battlefield Trust says that five days after the Battle of Johnstown, a group of Continentals and Oneida allies caught him alone in the wilderness and shot him dead. The Trust describes him as perhaps more responsible than anyone for the strife of the frontier war in New York, and also as its final victim.

In Cherry Valley Cemetery, on the line of the old fort, a vault about 8 feet high, 7 feet long and 5 feet wide holds the dead of the raid, Revolutionary War Journal says. It was unveiled on 15 August 1877. The extract from Greene's history places the monument at the centennial of the massacre, in 1878, and the two dates are not reconciled in the pages consulted. Its inscription lists soldiers killed and some of the roughly 32 settlers, among them the Wells family.
